content.title: About
content.content: Barbecue chicken consists of chicken pieces marinated in spices and barbecue sauce, then baked or grilled. The meat becomes aromatic, slightly sweet, and coated with a caramelized crust.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Barbecue originated in the United States, where meat was cooked over an open flame.
Chicken in barbecue sauce often carries smoky notes obtained with liquid smoke or actual smoking.
There are many regional barbecue sauce styles, from sweet tomato‑based to tangy vinegar‑based.
Chicken cooks faster than beef, making barbecue chicken a popular quick family dinner.
The combination of lean protein and spices provides a flavorful source of energy.

items.title: High‑quality protein
items.content: Chicken provides complete protein essential for muscle growth and tissue repair.

items.title: Low in saturated fat
items.content: Compared with red meat, chicken, especially skinless breast, contains less saturated fat.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Barbecue chicken supplies B3 (niacin) and B6, which support metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: Chicken is a source of phosphorus, selenium, and zinc, important for bones and immunity.

items.title: Antioxidant spices
items.content: Spices in the sauce (paprika, garlic, onion) have antioxidant properties.

items.title: Undercooking risk
items.content: Chicken must be fully cooked to avoid food‑borne illnesses such as salmonella.

items.title: Sugar in sauce
items.content: Barbecue sauce often contains added sugar, increasing calories and affecting blood glucose.

items.title: Spice allergies
items.content: Some individuals may be allergic to sauce ingredients like mustard or vinegar.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Sauces can be salty; those monitoring sodium should choose low‑salt versions.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Barbecue chicken can be served as a main dish, sliced into salads, used in sandwiches, tacos, or as a pizza topping. It pairs well with corn, potatoes, fresh vegetables, and light side sauces.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store cooked barbecue chicken in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. For longer storage, freeze portions in freezer‑safe bags for 2‑3 months. Reheat to an internal temperature of 75 °C before eating.

chicken-drumstick-baked-broiled-or-roast.title: Chicken Drumstick, Baked, Broiled, or Roasted, Skin Not Eaten

content.title: About
content.content: Skinless chicken drumsticks are the thigh meat of the bird, prepared by baking, broiling or roasting. Removing the skin reduces fat content while preserving a high amount of protein, B‑vitamins and minerals such as iron and zinc.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Drumsticks contain more iron than chicken breast because of the denser muscle fibers.
When cooked without skin, some fat renders out, which can make the meat drier; marinades or spices are often used to retain juiciness.
Chicken drumsticks are a staple in many cuisines, from American BBQ to Asian teriyaki dishes.
Thigh meat has a higher creatine content, supporting energy production in muscles.
Even without the skin, a well‑cooked drumstick can develop a pleasant crust when broiled.

items.title: High‑quality protein
items.content: A 100 g serving provides about 22 g of complete protein, essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Without skin the total fat drops to 3–4 g per 100 g, making it suitable for lower‑fat diets.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Rich in niacin (B3) and vitamin B6, which support metabolism and nervous‑system function.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: Provides iron, zinc and phosphorus, important for blood health, immunity and bone strength.

items.title: Creatine
items.content: Helps improve physical endurance and maintains cellular energy balance in muscles.

items.title: Poultry allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to chicken proteins.

items.title: Bacterial contamination
items.content: Raw chicken can harbor Salmonella or Campylobacter; cook to an internal temperature of 74 °C (165 °F) to ensure safety.

items.title: High sodium in marinades
items.content: Pre‑made marinades can be salty; monitor sodium intake if you have hypertension.

items.title: Dryness risk
items.content: Skinless drumsticks can become dry if overcooked; use a meat thermometer and avoid excessive cooking time.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Skinless drumsticks can be served as a main dish, sliced for salads, added to soups, or used in sandwiches. They pair well with herbs (rosemary, thyme), spices (paprika, garlic) and light sauces such as yogurt‑based dressings or lemon vinaigrette.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store raw meat in the refrigerator at + 1‑4 °C for up to 2 days. Cooked drumsticks keep in an airtight container in the fridge for up to 3 days or freeze for up to 3 months. Reheat cooked meat to an internal temperature of 74 °C before eating.

potato-from-puerto-rican-style-stuffed-p.title: Potato from Puerto Rican style stuffed pot roast, with gravy

content.title: About
content.content: This dish features a large potato baked until tender, stuffed with cubes of pot‑roast seasoned in a Puerto Rican style, and served with a rich gravy. The combination of creamy potato, juicy meat and aromatic sauce delivers a taste of the Caribbean.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Stuffing potatoes with meat dates back to Spanish colonies in the Caribbean.
Puerto Rican seasoning often includes adobo, oregano, garlic and lime, giving the dish its distinctive aroma.
The pot‑roast is usually cooked ahead of time and diced finely for even distribution inside the potato.
The gravy is made from chicken stock, cream and a touch of tomato paste, resulting in a thick, velvety sauce.
The dish is commonly served with fried plantains or rice and beans, staples of Puerto Rican cuisine.

items.title: Source of complex carbs
items.content: Potato provides sustained energy thanks to its high starch content.

items.title: Rich in vitamin C
items.content: Vitamin C supports the immune system and aids iron absorption.

items.title: Contains potassium
items.content: Potassium helps regulate blood pressure and muscle function.

items.title: Protein from pot‑roast
items.content: The meat adds complete protein needed for tissue repair.

items.title: Antioxidants from spices
items.content: Puerto Rican spices such as oregano and garlic contain antioxidants that combat free radicals.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: The gravy can be salty; people with hypertension should watch portion size.

items.title: Gluten allergy
items.content: If the gravy is thickened with wheat flour, it may pose a problem for those with celiac disease.

items.title: Saturated fat
items.content: Pot‑roast contains saturated fat; moderate consumption is advised for heart‑healthy diets.

items.title: Risk of overeating
items.content: The dish is calorie‑dense, so portions should be controlled, especially on weight‑loss plans.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve hot, cutting the potato in half and spooning the stuffing inside. Garnish with fresh herbs, a squeeze of lime, or a dash of hot sauce for extra zing. It pairs well with rice, beans or fried plantains.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Cool leftovers to room temperature, then store in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3 days. Reheat in the oven to retain the potato’s crisp skin.

content.title: About
content.content: Sandwich spread is a ready‑to‑eat paste made from plant‑based and/or dairy ingredients, designed for spreading on bread, rolls, and other baked goods. It has a smooth texture, mild flavor, and is often enriched with herbs, spices, and aromatics.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The first commercial sandwich spread appeared in the United States in the early 20th century as a cheaper alternative to butter.
More than 30 flavor variants exist: classic, garlic, herb, olive, cheese, and even sweet versions with berries.
Most modern spreads are vegan and contain no animal fats.
Sandwich spread is frequently used in making sandwiches, wraps, and canapé appetizers.

items.title: Rich in plant oils
items.content: Spreads based on olive or sunflower oil provide monounsaturated fats that support heart health.

items.title: Contains B‑vitamins
items.content: Formulations often include B1, B2, and B6 vitamins, which aid normal energy metabolism.

items.title: Antioxidant content
items.content: Herbs and spices such as rosemary and basil add antioxidant properties.

items.title: Convenient energy source
items.content: Its high calorie density makes it a quick source of energy, useful for active individuals.

items.title: Supports digestion
items.content: Some versions are fortified with probiotics or fermented ingredients that promote a healthy gut microbiome.

items.title: Allergy to ingredients
items.content: The product may contain nuts, soy, or dairy, which are common allergens.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Certain spreads contain up to 1 g of salt per 100 g, which may be unsuitable for hypertension.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: Because of its high energy density, portion control is advised, especially on weight‑management diets.

items.title: Preservatives
items.content: Some commercial spreads use artificial preservatives that can cause sensitivity in some people.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Spread it on bread, toast, baguette, or use as a filling for wraps and sandwiches. It can also be mixed into sauces, salad dressings, or used as a base for hot open‑face sandwiches.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the spread refrigerated at 2 °C–6 °C in its original packaging or an airtight container. After opening, use within 2–3 weeks. Discard if the smell, taste, or appearance changes or if mold appears.
